title: Imana, God of the Hills
summary: The supreme creator god who shaped the hills of Burundi with his hands, placing rivers in the valleys and forests on the slopes — and when the people forgot his name, the hills began to erode.
full_text:
Before the hills, there was only flatness.

The world was a plain — flat, featureless, endless. The sky hung above it like a lid on a pot. There were no valleys, no ridges, no places where the wind could hide. There was only the flat, and the sky, and the silence between them.

Imana looked at the flatness and was not satisfied. A world without hills is a world without secrets, without shelter, without the places where the rain collects and the roots grow deep.

Imana knelt. He placed his hands on the flat earth and pushed. The earth rose. It rose in waves, in ridges, in the rolling curves that would become the hills of Burundi. He pushed again, and the valleys appeared — deep, dark, cool, where the rivers would run and the forests would grow.

He planted the trees on the slopes — the cedars on the high ridges, the palms in the valleys, the fig trees where the water collected. He placed the animals in the forests — the antelope on the paths, the monkeys in the branches, the birds in the canopy.

He placed the people in the villages, in the valleys, where the soil was rich and the water was clean. He gave them cattle, and the cattle gave them milk. He gave them rain, and the rain gave them crops.

Imana told the people: Remember my name. When you remember my name, the hills will stand. When you forget, the hills will fall.

The people remembered. For generations, they remembered. They called Imana's name when the rain came, when the harvest was good, when the cattle bore calves. They called his name when the hills were green, when the rivers ran clear, when the forests were thick.

But the people forgot. They forgot because they were busy, because the world was changing, because the hills had always been there and would always be there.

The hills began to erode. The rain cut channels in the slopes. The rivers ran brown with soil. The forests thinned. The paths washed away.

The people remembered. They called Imana's name. They poured libations on the earth. They left offerings on the hilltops.

Imana heard. The erosion slowed. The rivers cleared. The forests grew.

But the hills were not as tall as they had been. The valleys were not as deep. The world was a little flatter than Imana had made it.

Imana is still in the hills. He is still pushing, still shaping, still trying to keep the world from flattening.

The people still call his name.
moral: When we forget the names of the things that hold us up, they begin to fall.
source: Burundi creation oral tradition, documented by Frédéric Ntidendabenga

title: the Imizimu, the Ancestors Who Walk
summary: The spirits of the dead who walk among the living, visible only in the flicker of a candle flame — because in Burundi, death does not end the conversation.
full_text:
The Imizimu are the ancestors.

They are not dead. They are not alive. They are in between — in the space where the living world ends and the other world begins. They walk among the living, but they are invisible. You cannot see them with your eyes. You can only see them with the flame.

When a candle flickers in a room where no wind blows, the Imizimu are passing. When a flame gutters and flares, the Imizimu are speaking. When a fire dies suddenly, without reason, the Imizimu are angry.

The Burundian people do not fear the Imizimu. They respect them. The Imizimu are the ancestors — the mothers, the fathers, the grandparents, the great-grandparents. They are the ones who built the villages, who cleared the fields, who raised the cattle. They are the ones whose hands shaped the world that the living inherit.

The Imizimu do not haunt. They visit. They come to the houses where their descendants live. They come to the ceremonies, the births, the marriages, the funerals. They come to the fireside, where the family gathers at night.

You cannot see them. But you can feel them. The warmth of the fire increases. The air grows heavier. The candle flame flickers.

When the Imizimu are pleased, the family prospers. The cattle bear calves. The crops grow tall. The children are healthy.

When the Imizimu are displeased, the family suffers. The cattle sicken. The crops fail. The children fall ill.

The only way to please the Imizimu is to remember them. Speak their names. Tell their stories. Pour libations at their graves. Leave offerings of food and beer where the candle flame flickers.

The Imizimu are patient. They will wait for the living to remember. They will visit, night after night, candle flame after candle flame, until the names are spoken and the stories are told.

The Imizimu are still walking. They are still visiting. They are still waiting.

The candle flame flickers.
moral: The dead do not leave. They visit, and they wait for us to remember.
source: Burundi ancestor worship tradition, documented by Jean-Pierre Harroy

title: the Tanganyika Serpent, the Lake's Guardian
summary: A massive serpent that lives in the deepest waters of Lake Tanganyika, stirring the currents that bring fish to the shore — and when it sleeps, the lake goes still and the fishermen catch nothing.
full_text:
Lake Tanganyika is deep. No one has found the bottom. The water is so clear that you can see fifty meters down, and then the blue darkness swallows the light and the fish disappear.

In the deep water, beneath the light, beneath the thermocline, beneath the place where the water changes from warm to cold, there is a serpent.

The serpent is old. It was old when the lake was young. It was old when the hills that surround the lake were flat. It was old when the first fisherman cast his net from a dugout canoe.

The serpent is large. Its body coils through the deep water, winding between the submerged ridges, circling the underwater canyons. Its head rests on the lakebed, its eyes closed, its mouth slightly open. Its breath is the current that brings fish to the shore.

When the serpent breathes, the water moves. The current rises from the deep, carrying nutrients, carrying plankton, carrying the small fish that feed the big fish that feed the fishermen. The fishermen cast their nets. The nets are heavy. The canoes ride low.

When the serpent sleeps, the water is still. No current rises from the deep. No nutrients reach the surface. The fish stay in the deep, where the water is cold and dark. The fishermen cast their nets. The nets are empty. The canoes return light.

The fishermen of Burundi know the serpent. They do not see it — it is too deep. But they feel it. They feel the current, or the lack of it. They feel the weight of the nets, or the emptiness.

When the lake is still for too long — when the current does not rise, when the fish do not come — the fishermen go to the shore and call the serpent's name. They do not know the name — no one knows the name. They call: "O serpent of the deep, wake. The fishermen are hungry."

Sometimes, the serpent hears. The current rises. The fish come. The nets are heavy.

Sometimes, the serpent does not hear. The lake remains still. The fishermen wait.

The serpent sleeps. The lake waits. The fishermen cast their nets and hope.
moral: The life we harvest depends on the sleep of the deep.
source: Burundi lakeside fishing communities oral tradition

title: the Mountain Giant, Keeper of the Peaks
summary: A giant made of stone and moss that lives on the highest peak of the Congo-Nile ridge, pushing the clouds aside with its hands — and when it rests, the fog covers the mountains for days.
full_text:
The Congo-Nile ridge runs through Burundi like a spine. It divides the country in two — the rivers that flow west to the Congo, and the rivers that flow east to the Nile. The ridge is high, the air is thin, and the clouds hang low.

On the highest peak of the ridge, where the air is too thin for trees and the ground is covered in moss, there is a giant.

The giant is made of stone. Its body is the mountain itself — its legs are the ridges, its arms are the cliffs, its head is the peak. Moss grows on its shoulders. Lichen covers its face. Its eyes are two boulders, round and dark, watching the valleys below.

The giant pushes the clouds. When the clouds pile up on the ridge, blocking the sun, drowning the valleys in fog, the giant lifts its arms and pushes. The clouds part. The sun comes through. The valleys are warm again.

But the giant is old. It is tired. The pushing is heavy. The clouds are relentless. Every day, the clouds come, and every day, the giant pushes them back.

When the giant rests — when it lowers its arms and closes its boulder eyes — the fog covers the mountains. It settles in the valleys, in the forests, in the paths that the shepherds walk. The shepherds cannot see. The cattle stray. The villages are cut off.

The villagers do not panic. They know the giant is resting. They wait. They sit by their fires and tell stories. They wait for the giant to open its eyes and push the clouds back.

Sometimes, the giant rests for a day. Sometimes, for three days. Sometimes, for a week. The fog thickens. The world disappears.

But the giant always wakes. It always pushes. The clouds always part. The sun always comes through.

The villagers do not thank the giant. They do not leave offerings on the peak — the peak is too high, too dangerous, too remote. They simply wait, and when the fog lifts, they return to their fields, their cattle, their lives.

The giant pushes. The clouds part. The sun comes through.

The giant rests. The fog returns. The villagers wait.
moral: The giants who hold up our sky are not always awake. Sometimes we must wait in the fog.

title: the Night-Walker, Shadow of the Savanna
summary: A shadow that walks the savanna at night, taking the shape of anyone who has ever died — and if you see it, it will take your shape next, so that someone, someday, will see you walking where you have never been.
full_text:
The Night-Walker is a shadow.

Not the shadow of a person, not the shadow of a tree, not the shadow of anything that stands in the sun. The Night-Walker is a shadow that exists on its own — a darkness that moves without a source, that walks without feet, that breathes without lungs.

The Night-Walker takes shapes. It can be anyone — anyone who has ever died. It can be your mother, your father, your grandfather, your neighbor. It wears their face, their clothes, their walk. It speaks with their voice, their accent, their pauses.

The Night-Walker walks the savanna at night. It moves between the termite mounds, past the acacia trees, along the paths that the cattle walk during the day. It moves slowly, carefully, as if it is looking for someone.

Sometimes, a herder returning home at dusk sees the Night-Walker. He sees his dead father, walking across the savanna, heading toward the village. He calls out: "Father! Father, wait!" He runs toward the figure.

The figure does not wait. It keeps walking. The herder follows. He follows past the termite mounds, past the acacia trees, past the path that leads home.

He follows until the savanna is dark and the village is far away. He follows until the figure stops. He follows until the figure turns.

The figure is no longer his father. It is him. It has his face, his clothes, his walk. It looks at him with his own eyes.

The herder runs. He runs back to the village. He arrives breathless, wild-eyed, shaking. He tells his family: I saw myself on the savanna.

The family does not believe him. They say: You were tired. You were confused. You saw a tree, or a mound, or the moon.

But the herder knows. He saw himself. The Night-Walker took his shape. And now, somewhere on the savanna, a shadow wears his face and walks where he has never been.

The Night-Walker is still walking. It is still taking shapes. It is still looking for someone.

If you walk the savanna at night, and you see someone you know — someone who is dead, someone who should not be there — do not follow. Turn around. Walk home. Do not look back.

The Night-Walker is patient. It will find someone to follow.
moral: Some shadows are not cast by the living.

title: Kiranga, the Sacred Drum
summary: A drum that beats on its own at midnight, its rhythm echoing across the hills — because the drum holds the heartbeat of the first king, and as long as it beats, the kingdom endures.
full_text:
The Kiranga is not a drum. It is a heartbeat.

It was carved from the wood of the first umuvumu tree — the fig tree that grew at the center of the world, where the first king of Burundi sat and listened to the earth. The wood was old, dense, resonant. When the carver struck it, the sound did not die. It echoed. It bounced between the hills. It traveled across the valleys. It reached the sky.

The carver made the drum. He stretched the skin of a sacred bull over the opening. He tuned it with the pitch of the wind. And when the first king struck the drum, it did not sound like a drum.

It sounded like a heartbeat.

The king placed the drum in the center of the kingdom, in a hut made of sacred wood, guarded by the oldest warriors. He told the drum: Beat. Beat for the kingdom. Beat for the people. Beat for the hills.

The drum beat. It beat every midnight, without a drummer, without a stick, without a hand. It beat with the heartbeat of the first king, which the wood had stored when the king struck it.

As long as the drum beat, the kingdom endured. The hills stood. The rivers ran. The cattle bore calves. The people prospered.

The drum beat for centuries. It beat through wars, through famines, through the long droughts that turned the hills brown. It beat through the arrival of the Europeans, the missionaries, the administrators. It beat through independence, through celebration, through grief.

The drum still beats. Every midnight, in the hut of sacred wood, the Kiranga beats. The warriors guard it. The people listen. The hills stand.

Some say the drum will beat forever. Some say it will stop when the last king dies. Some say it will stop when the last person forgets the name of the first king.

The drum beats. The kingdom endures. The hills stand.

The midnight comes. The drum beats.
moral: A kingdom endures as long as its heartbeat is heard.
source: Burundi royal court tradition, documented by Antoine van Gennep

title: the Imandwa, Spirits of the Hill
summary: Spirits that live in the tallest hills, appearing as balls of light at dusk — because in Burundi, every hill has a guardian, and the guardian demands respect.
full_text:
The Imandwa live on the hilltops.

They are not visible in daylight. They are not visible in the dark. They are visible only at dusk — in the space between day and night, when the sky is purple and the hills are shadows.

At dusk, the Imandwa appear. They appear as balls of light — not fire, not lightning, not the flash of a firefly. The light is steady, soft, the color of milk. It hovers above the hilltop, three or four feet above the ground, and it does not move.

The villagers see the light. They know what it is. They do not approach. The Imandwa are the spirits of the hill — the guardians, the keepers, the ones who ensure that the rain falls on the right fields, that the wind comes from the right direction, that the crops grow on the right slopes.

The Imandwa do not speak. They do not move. They simply watch. They watch the village, the fields, the cattle. They watch for respect.

When the villagers show respect — when they leave offerings on the hilltop, when they do not cut the trees on the sacred slope, when they do not hunt the animals on the sacred path — the Imandwa are pleased. The rain falls on the fields. The crops grow tall. The cattle bear calves.

When the villagers do not show respect — when they cut the trees, when they hunt the animals, when they leave the hilltop littered with waste — the Imandwa are displeased. The rain falls on the wrong fields. The crops fail. The cattle sicken.

The only way to restore the Imandwa's favor is to climb the hill at dusk, when the light appears. Leave an offering: a calabash of beer, a bundle of bananas, a strand of cowrie shells. Do not look at the light. Do not speak to the light. Simply leave the offering and descend.

The Imandwa accept the offering. The light flickers — not brighter, not dimmer, but differently. The flicker is the Imandwa saying: We see you. We accept. You may go.

The villager descends the hill. The light fades. The night comes.

The Imandwa are still there. They are always there. They watch from the hilltops. They wait for respect.
moral: Every hill has a guardian, and every guardian demands respect.

title: Imana and the First Rain
summary: When the world was dry and the rivers were empty, Imana struck the sky with his staff and the first rain fell — but the rain was a gift, not a right, and it can be taken back.
full_text:
The world was dry.

The rivers were empty. The lakes were low. The hills were brown. The cattle stood in the shade and did not move. The people sat in their houses and did not speak. The dust rose from the ground and hung in the air, thick and choking.

Imana looked at the world and was not satisfied. He had made the hills, the valleys, the rivers, the forests. He had made the people, the cattle, the crops. But he had not made the rain.

The rain was in the sky. It had always been in the sky. But the sky was sealed — closed like a lid, tight like a drum. The rain could not fall. The water could not reach the earth.

Imana took his staff. It was a long staff, made of the wood of the umuvumu tree, the fig tree that grew at the center of the world. He held it above his head and struck the sky.

The sky cracked. The crack was narrow — as narrow as a hair, as thin as a wire. But the rain came through. It fell in drops, then in sheets, then in the kind of rain that turns the dust to mud and the rivers to torrents.

The world drank. The rivers filled. The lakes rose. The hills turned green. The cattle moved from the shade to the pasture. The people came from their houses and stood in the rain and let it wash the dust from their skin.

Imana told the people: The rain is a gift. It is not a right. It comes because I have struck the sky. It comes because I have opened the crack. It comes because I choose to give it.

If you forget my name, I will close the crack. If you forget my name, the rain will stop. If you forget my name, the world will dry again.

The people remembered. For generations, they remembered. They called Imana's name when the rain came. They poured libations on the earth. They left offerings on the hilltops.

But the people forgot. And Imana closed the crack.

The rain stopped. The rivers fell. The hills turned brown.

The people remembered. They called Imana's name. They poured libations. They left offerings.

Imana opened the crack. The rain fell.

The crack is still there. The rain still falls. But the crack is narrow, and Imana's hand is on the staff.

The rain is a gift.
moral: Rain is a gift, not a right. It can be given, and it can be taken.
